seo.title: Buy vs Rent Calculator: Break-Even Year & Net Worth Comparison
seo.description: Free buy vs rent calculator. Compare mortgage, tax, upkeep and opportunity cost against rent to see your break-even year and net worth after 1 to 40 years.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Compare the true long-term cost of owning a home against renting and investing the difference.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Deciding whether to buy a home or keep renting is one of the biggest financial choices most people make. The monthly mortgage payment is only part of the picture. Owners also pay property tax, insurance, maintenance and, eventually, selling costs, while renters keep their down payment free to invest.

This calculator models both paths month by month. It tracks the owner's home equity and the renter's investment portfolio, then shows which side has more net worth after the number of years you plan to stay. It also finds the break-even year, the first year in which buying overtakes renting.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home price, down payment, mortgage rate and loan term.
Add ownership costs: property tax, insurance, maintenance, closing and selling costs.
Enter your current rent and the rent increase you expect each year.
Set the investment return a renter could earn on the money that would otherwise go into the house.
Choose how many years you expect to stay and read the verdict, chart and table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Buyer net worth = home value × (1 − selling cost %) − remaining loan balance
Renter net worth = (down payment + closing costs) invested, plus every month the owner's total cost exceeds rent, invested at your chosen return
Monthly cost to own = mortgage payment + (property tax + insurance + maintenance) ÷ 12
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: Take a $450,000 home with 20% down, a 6.5% 30-year mortgage, 1.1% property tax, $1,800 insurance and 1% maintenance, compared with $2,400 monthly rent. With 3% annual appreciation and 6% investment returns, buying is still behind after five years because closing and selling costs are high, but it moves ahead later in the second decade as the loan is paid down and the home appreciates. Try different horizons to see how sensitive the result is to how long you stay.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
The longer you stay, the more buying tends to win, because upfront and selling costs are spread over more years.
High mortgage rates and low rent-to-price ratios favor renting. Low rates and fast rent growth favor buying.
Be honest about maintenance. Older homes often cost more than 1% of value each year.
Test a pessimistic case with zero appreciation to see how much of the result depends on price growth.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: Is it better to buy or rent a home?
default.a: Neither is always better. Buying usually pays off when you stay many years, can afford a sizeable down payment and buy at a reasonable price relative to rent. Renting often wins for short stays, high prices or when you can invest the savings well. This calculator compares both using your own numbers.

default.q: What is the break-even point when buying vs renting?
default.a: It is the first year in which the owner's net worth (home equity after selling costs) is at least as large as the renter's investment portfolio. Before that year renting has been the cheaper path overall.

default.q: Does this calculator include tax deductions?
default.a: No. It does not model mortgage interest or property tax deductions, because many households take the standard deduction. Including deductions would make buying look somewhat better for those who itemize.

default.q: What investment return should I assume for the renter?
default.a: A long-run balanced portfolio has historically returned roughly 5% to 7% a year before inflation adjustments. Use a lower number if you would keep the money in savings, and a higher one only if you are comfortable with the risk.

default.q: Is a house a good investment?
default.a: A home provides housing, forced savings through loan payments and potential appreciation, but it also carries costs and concentrated risk. Compare it against alternatives with this tool rather than assuming it always beats renting.

seo.title: Rental Property ROI Calculator: Cap Rate, Cash Flow & Cash-on-Cash
seo.description: Free rental property ROI calculator. Enter price, rent and expenses to get cap rate, cash-on-cash return, monthly cash flow, DSCR and break-even occupancy.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Check cap rate, cash-on-cash return, cash flow and debt coverage before you buy a rental.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A rental property can look attractive on listing sites and still lose money once taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancy and the mortgage are counted. This rental property ROI calculator turns the asking price and expected rent into the metrics investors and lenders actually use.

You get the cap rate, the cash-on-cash return on the money you put in, monthly cash flow, the debt service coverage ratio and a breakdown of where each year's rent goes.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, down payment, closing costs and loan terms.
Enter expected monthly rent and a realistic vacancy rate.
Add property tax, insurance, repairs and management costs.
Review cash flow, cap rate, cash-on-cash return and DSCR, then adjust inputs to stress-test the deal.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Net operating income (NOI) = collected rent − taxes − insurance − repairs − management
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Cash flow = NOI − annual loan payments
Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow ÷ (down payment + closing costs)
DSCR = NOI ÷ annual loan payments
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A $300,000 duplex rents for $2,500 a month with 5% vacancy, $3,600 tax, $1,500 insurance, 5% repairs and 8% management. With 25% down at 6.75%, NOI is about $19,620 and the cap rate is about 6.5%. After loan payments, cash flow is only about $176 a month, a 2.5% cash-on-cash return on $84,000 invested, and the debt service coverage ratio is about 1.12, below the 1.25 many lenders look for. Raising rent by $200 a month or negotiating the price shows how quickly those numbers move.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Never assume zero vacancy or zero repairs. Even good tenants leave and roofs wear out.
Lenders typically want a DSCR of at least 1.2 to 1.25.
Cap rate ignores financing, while cash-on-cash includes it. Look at both.
Check rent assumptions against local listings rather than the seller's pro forma.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is a good ROI on a rental property?
default.a: Many investors target a cash-on-cash return of 8% or more and a cap rate that matches or beats the local market. What is good for you depends on risk, location and your alternatives.

default.q: What is the difference between cap rate and cash-on-cash return?
default.a: Cap rate measures property income against the full price as if bought with cash. Cash-on-cash return measures your actual annual cash flow against the cash you invested, so it reflects your loan.

default.q: What expenses should I include?
default.a: Include property tax, insurance, a repair and maintenance reserve, management fees (even if you self-manage), vacancy, and any HOA or utilities you pay. Do not include loan principal in operating expenses.

default.q: What is the 1% rule?
default.a: A rule of thumb that says monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price. It is a quick screen, not a substitute for running the full numbers.

seo.title: Real Estate ROI Calculator: Total Return with Appreciation
seo.description: Free real estate ROI calculator. Project cash flow, equity and appreciation over your holding period to see total ROI and annualized return on cash invested.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: See total return including cash flow, loan paydown and appreciation over your holding period.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Rental income is only one source of real estate returns. Over a multi-year hold you also build equity as the loan is paid down and benefit, or suffer, from changes in the property's value. This calculator combines all three.

It projects each year's cash flow, estimates your net equity after selling costs, and reports the total ROI and the annualized return on the cash you invested.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, financing and closing costs.
Enter starting rent, expected rent growth and an operating expense ratio.
Set your expected appreciation, selling costs and how many years you will hold.
Read total ROI, annualized return and the year-by-year projection.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Total position = equity after selling costs + cumulative cash flow
Total ROI = (total position − cash invested) ÷ cash invested
Annualized return = (total position ÷ cash invested)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: Buying a $350,000 property with 20% down, 3% closing costs, $2,600 rent growing 3% a year and 40% operating costs, then selling after ten years at 3% appreciation and 6% selling costs, turns about $80,500 of cash invested into roughly $200,000 of equity after selling costs plus accumulated cash flow. That is a total ROI of about 148%, or roughly 9.5% a year. Cash flow is slightly negative in the early years, so the return comes mostly from loan paydown and appreciation. Raising or lowering appreciation shows how much of the result depends on market growth.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use conservative appreciation. Long-run national averages are often quoted around 3% to 4%, but local markets vary.
Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. Try a lower down payment to see the effect.
This calculator does not model income tax, depreciation or major capital repairs.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate ROI on real estate?
default.a: Add the property's cumulative cash flow to the equity you would receive at sale, subtract the cash you originally invested, and divide by that cash. This tool does it for you year by year.

default.q: Is annualized return better than total ROI?
default.a: Annualized return lets you compare properties held for different lengths of time and compare real estate with other investments such as index funds.

default.q: Does the calculator include taxes?
default.a: No. Income tax, depreciation recapture and capital gains vary by situation, so consult a tax professional for after-tax results.

seo.title: Cap Rate Calculator: Capitalization Rate & Property Value
seo.description: Free cap rate calculator. Enter price, rent, vacancy and operating expenses to get NOI, capitalization rate, gross rent multiplier and value at the market cap rate.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Calculate capitalization rate and estimate what a property is worth at the market cap rate.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
The capitalization rate, or cap rate, is the annual income a property produces as a percentage of its price, ignoring financing. It lets you compare properties of different sizes and check whether an asking price is in line with the market.

This calculator works out net operating income from rent, vacancy and expenses, then shows the cap rate and the value implied by a market cap rate you choose.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price and monthly gross rent.
Set a vacancy allowance and annual operating expenses (without loan payments).
Enter the cap rate typical for similar properties in the area.
Compare the property's cap rate with the market, and the implied value with the asking price.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
NOI = gross rent × (1 − vacancy) − operating expenses
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Implied value = NOI ÷ market cap rate
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A building priced at $800,000 collects $7,500 a month, has 5% vacancy and $30,000 of annual operating costs. After vacancy, rent is $85,500 a year, so NOI is $55,500 and the cap rate is about 6.94%. If similar buildings trade at a 6% cap rate, the implied value is $925,000, which suggests the asking price is attractive, assuming the income figures are reliable.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Cap rate is only as reliable as the NOI behind it. Verify rents and expenses with documents.

fields.label: Tagline

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Cash-on-cash return answers a practical question: for every dollar of your own money in the deal, how many dollars of cash flow do you get back each year? Because it counts only the cash you invested, it shows the effect of leverage that cap rate hides.

This calculator adds up your down payment, closing costs and upfront repairs, subtracts loan payments from net income, and shows a rent sensitivity table so you can see how fragile the return is.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the price, down payment, closing costs and any upfront repair budget.
Enter the loan rate and term.
Enter monthly rent and operating expenses as a percentage of rent.
Read the return and use the sensitivity table to test lower or higher rent.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Annual cash flow = rent × 12 × (1 − expense ratio) − annual loan payments
Cash invested = down payment + closing costs + upfront repairs
Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow ÷ cash invested
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: On a $275,000 rental with 25% down, 3% closing, $5,000 of repairs, a 7% loan and $2,400 rent with 40% expenses, you invest about $82,000. Annual cash flow after the mortgage is only about $814, a return of roughly 1.0% with a debt service coverage ratio of 1.05, well under the common 8% target. The sensitivity table shows how fragile that is: 5% lower rent turns cash flow slightly negative, while 10% higher rent lifts the return to about 3.1%.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Include every dollar of upfront cash, including repairs, not just the down payment.
An 8% to 12% cash-on-cash return is a common target, but risk and location matter as much as the number.
A very high return from a tiny cash investment can hide large risk. Look at DSCR too.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is cash on cash return?
default.a: It is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by the total cash you invested in the property. It focuses on the return on your own money rather than the property's total value.

default.q: What is a good cash on cash return?
default.a: Many investors aim for 8% to 12%, though the right target depends on risk, market and alternatives such as index funds.

default.q: How is it different from ROI?
default.a: Cash-on-cash return looks only at yearly cash flow. ROI can also include appreciation and loan paydown over the whole holding period. Use the Real Estate ROI calculator for the broader view.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate profit, return on cash and the 70% rule maximum offer before you buy a flip.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
House flipping margins are thinner than they look. Between the purchase, the rehab, loan interest and points, holding costs, and agent fees at sale, a deal that seems to leave $100,000 on paper can end up with a fraction of that.

This calculator adds every cost, subtracts it from the after-repair value (ARV), and shows your net profit, the return on the cash you actually put in, and the maximum offer implied by the common 70% rule.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, rehab budget and the ARV based on recent comparable sales.
Set how many months you expect the project to take from closing to sale.
Add your loan terms: percent financed, interest rate and points. Use 0% financed for an all-cash flip.
Enter buying closing costs, monthly holding costs and selling costs.
Check the profit, return and 70% rule offer, then test a longer timeline or a higher rehab cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Total cost = purchase + rehab + buying costs + loan interest + points + holding costs + selling costs
Net profit = ARV − total cost
Return on cash = net profit ÷ cash you invested
70% rule maximum offer = ARV × 70% − rehab cost
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: Suppose you buy at $200,000, spend $45,000 on rehab, and expect an ARV of $330,000 after six months. With an 80% hard-money loan at 11% plus 2 points, $1,200 monthly holding costs and 7% selling costs, the net profit is about $38,700 on $108,200 of your own cash (a 36% return), far smaller than the $85,000 gap between ARV and purchase plus rehab. Extending the project from six to nine months cuts profit to about $30,700, which is why timelines matter so much.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Be conservative with ARV. Use sold comps within a mile and the last six months, not listing prices.
Add a contingency of 10% to 15% to the rehab budget. Surprises are normal.
Every extra month adds interest, taxes, insurance and utilities. Test slower timelines.
The 70% rule is a screen, not a guarantee. In expensive markets investors may accept a higher percentage.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is the 70% rule in house flipping?
default.a: It says an investor should pay no more than 70% of the after-repair value minus the cost of repairs. For an ARV of $300,000 and $40,000 of repairs, the maximum offer is $170,000.

default.q: How much profit should a flip make?
default.a: Many investors look for at least $25,000 to $30,000 or a 15% to 20% return on cash per project, because flips carry risk of delays, cost overruns and price drops.

default.q: What costs do people forget when flipping?
default.a: Loan points and interest, holding costs like utilities and insurance, permits, dumpsters, staging, and seller closing costs are commonly underestimated.

default.q: Does this include taxes on the profit?
default.a: No. Flip profits are often taxed as ordinary income. Talk to a tax professional about your situation.

Many first-time buyers save for the down payment and are surprised by closing costs on top of it. These are the fees and prepaid items due when the sale completes, and they commonly run between 2% and 5% of the home price.

Enter the home price and your planned down payment percentage.

fields.default:

Title and escrow = price × title %
Prepaids = (annual tax + annual insurance) ÷ 12 × prepaid months

fields.help: One formula per line.

default.q: How much are closing costs on a house?

default.q: Are closing costs included in the down payment?

default.q: Who pays closing costs, the buyer or seller?
default.a: Both pay some costs. Buyers usually pay lender, title and prepaid items. Sellers typically pay agent commissions and transfer-related charges, depending on local custom and negotiation.

default.q: Can I reduce my closing costs?
default.a: Yes. Compare lenders, ask about fee waivers, shop for title and insurance, negotiate seller concessions, and avoid buying discount points if you may sell soon.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Build a simple income statement for an income property and see NOI, cap rate and debt coverage.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Net operating income is the number that drives commercial property value and loan approval. It is the income a property produces after vacancy and operating expenses, before the mortgage, depreciation and income taxes.

This calculator builds a simple annual income statement from rent, other income and your expense lines. It reports NOI, the expense ratio, the cap rate on your purchase price, and the debt service coverage ratio lenders look at.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter scheduled monthly rent and any other income such as parking or laundry.
Set a vacancy and credit loss percentage.
Enter annual tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance, and a management percentage.
Add the purchase price and loan terms to see cap rate and debt coverage.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Effective gross income = (rent + other income) × 12 × (1 − vacancy)
NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
DSCR = NOI ÷ annual loan payments
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A building collecting $24,000 monthly rent and $1,200 of other income with 7% vacancy, $67,000 of fixed annual costs and 5% management produces an NOI of about $200,000. On a $2.8 million price that is a cap rate near 7.2%. With a 70% loan at 6.75% over 25 years, the debt coverage ratio is about 1.23, just under the 1.25 many lenders want, so a lender might ask for a lower loan amount.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Do not include mortgage payments, depreciation or income tax in operating expenses.
Use actual operating statements from the seller and verify them against bills and leases.
Include a repair and capital reserve even if the seller does not.
Compare the expense ratio with similar buildings. A very low ratio can mean missing costs.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is NOI in real estate?
default.a: Net operating income is a property's income after vacancy and operating expenses, but before debt service, depreciation and income taxes.

default.q: Is NOI the same as cash flow?
default.a: No. Cash flow is what remains after paying the loan. NOI is calculated before loan payments, so it describes the property rather than the financing.

default.q: What is a good DSCR?
default.a: Lenders often require 1.20 to 1.35 for commercial loans. A higher ratio means more cushion above the loan payments.

default.q: What is a normal expense ratio?
default.a: It varies by property type, but many multifamily properties run between about 35% and 50% of effective income.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate your annual and monthly property tax and see how it could grow over the years.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Property tax is one of the largest ongoing costs of owning a home, and it varies enormously by location. Effective rates range from roughly 0.3% of value in a few low-tax areas to above 2% in several high-tax states, which can mean thousands of dollars a year on the same priced home.

This calculator multiplies taxable value by your local effective rate, subtracts exemptions, and projects how the bill could change as assessed value rises.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home's assessed or market value.
Enter the effective tax rate from your county tax bill or assessor website.
Add any exemptions that reduce taxable value, such as a homestead exemption.
Set how fast assessed value is expected to rise and how many years to project.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Taxable value = home value − exemptions
Annual property tax = taxable value × effective tax rate
Monthly property tax = annual tax ÷ 12
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A $400,000 home with a 1.1% effective rate and no exemptions owes about $4,400 a year, or $367 a month. If assessed value rises 3% annually, the bill passes $5,700 by year ten. A $50,000 homestead exemption would lower the starting bill by $550 a year.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use the effective rate (tax divided by market value), not the nominal millage rate, unless you convert it properly.
New buyers are sometimes reassessed at the purchase price, so the previous owner's bill can understate yours.
Check for exemptions and appeal options. Assessments can contain errors.
Escrow accounts collect property tax monthly with your mortgage payment.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How is property tax calculated?
default.a: Local governments multiply the taxable value of the property by the combined tax rate set by counties, cities and school districts, after any exemptions are removed.

default.q: What is an effective property tax rate?
default.a: It is the annual tax bill divided by the home's market value. It makes areas comparable even when assessment methods and millage rates differ.

default.q: Can I lower my property tax?
default.a: Often yes. Apply for exemptions you qualify for and appeal the assessment if you believe it exceeds market value, following your county's deadline.

default.q: Why did my property tax go up?
default.a: Common reasons are a higher assessed value, new voter-approved levies, the end of a temporary exemption or a reassessment after a sale or renovation.

Compare monthly savings, break-even months and net savings over time.

Monthly savings = current payment − new payment
Break-even months = closing costs ÷ monthly savings

fields.help: One formula per line.

default.a: Divide the closing costs by the monthly savings. With $6,000 of costs and $300 monthly savings, break-even takes about 20 months.

default.a: A lender's credit check can cause a small, temporary dip, and a new account changes your credit mix. The effect is usually modest.

default.q: Should I choose a shorter term?
default.a: A shorter term has a higher payment but saves interest and builds equity faster. Choose based on what payment you can comfortably afford.

seo.title: Gravel Calculator: Cubic Yards, Tons & Cost
seo.description: Free gravel calculator. Enter length, width and depth to get cubic yards, tons, bags and estimated cost, with an editable material weight and price.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out how many cubic yards, tons and bags of gravel you need for any rectangular area.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Ordering the right amount of gravel saves a second delivery fee and a half-finished project. Suppliers sell gravel by the ton or the cubic yard, but you measure your project in feet and inches, so a conversion is needed.

This calculator turns length, width and depth into cubic yards, tons, and 0.5 cubic foot bags, adds an allowance for settling, and estimates cost from your local price per ton.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Measure the length and width of the area in feet.
Enter the depth in inches. Paths often use 2 to 3 inches, driveways 4 to 8 inches in layers.
Adjust the material weight if your supplier gives a different figure.
Enter your delivered price per ton to see the cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Cubic feet = length × width × depth in inches ÷ 12
Cubic yards = cubic feet ÷ 27, plus an allowance for settling
Tons = cubic yards × material weight (about 1.4 tons per yard for gravel)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: For a 20 ft × 10 ft area covered 3 inches deep with a 5% allowance, you need about 1.94 cubic yards, or 2.72 tons at 1.4 tons per yard. At $40 a ton that is roughly $109. The table on the page shows the same area at other depths, which helps you compare options before ordering.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Order slightly more than you need. A small top-up delivery often costs more than extra material.
Ask the supplier for the actual weight per cubic yard of the product you are buying.
Compact the base before adding the next layer, and order extra for compaction on driveways.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.

default.q: How do I calculate how much gravel I need?

default.q: How many tons are in a cubic yard of gravel?
default.a: Most gravel and crushed stone weighs between 1.3 and 1.5 tons per cubic yard, about 2,600 to 3,000 pounds. Wet or fine material can be heavier.

default.q: How deep should gravel be?
default.a: Walkways and garden paths commonly use 2 to 3 inches. Patio bases use 4 to 6 inches, and driveways use 6 to 8 inches built in layers.

default.q: Should I order by the ton or by the yard?
default.a: Either works if you know the conversion. Many quarries sell by the ton, while landscape yards often sell by the cubic yard. Compare the delivered price per ton using this calculator.

seo.title: Gravel Driveway Calculator: Tons, Layers & Cost
seo.description: Free gravel driveway calculator. Enter length, width and layer depths to estimate tons of base and surface stone, cubic yards, delivery and total cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate base and surface stone, tons and cost for a new or refreshed gravel driveway.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A durable gravel driveway is built in layers: a coarse base for strength, and a finer surface layer that locks together. Each layer needs a different stone and quantity, so a single depth estimate often leads to under-ordering.

This calculator works out both layers from your driveway size, adds an allowance for compaction, and totals the cost including delivery.

fields.default:
Enter the length and width of the driveway.
Set the base layer depth and the surface layer depth in inches.
Add an allowance for compaction, typically 10% to 20%.
Enter prices per ton for each stone and your delivery charges.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Layer cubic yards = length × width × depth in inches ÷ 12 ÷ 27 × (1 + compaction)
Layer tons = cubic yards × material weight
Total cost = base cost + surface cost + delivery
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A 60 ft × 12 ft driveway (720 sq ft) with a 4 inch base and a 2 inch surface layer, plus 15% for compaction, needs about 14.3 tons of base stone and 7.2 tons of surface stone: roughly 21.5 tons in all. At $35 and $42 a ton plus $150 delivery, the estimate is about $951, or $1.32 per square foot.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Good drainage matters more than thickness. Crown the driveway and keep water from pooling.
A geotextile fabric under the base helps on soft soil and keeps layers from mixing.
Expect to top up the surface every few years as stone migrates.

default.q: How much gravel do I need for a driveway?
default.a: Multiply length by width by depth to get volume, convert to cubic yards, then to tons. A 60 × 12 ft driveway at a total depth of 6 inches needs roughly 20 tons including compaction.

default.q: What size gravel is best for a driveway?

default.q: How thick should a gravel driveway be?
default.a: Most are 6 to 8 inches thick in total, built in two or three compacted layers. Soft soil or heavy vehicles call for more.

default.q: Why order extra gravel for a driveway?
default.a: Loose stone compacts when rolled and some is lost into the subsoil, so adding 10% to 20% avoids a shortfall.

seo.title: French Drain Calculator: Gravel, Pipe & Fabric Needed
seo.description: Free French drain calculator. Enter trench length, width, depth and pipe size to estimate tons of gravel, feet of pipe, filter fabric and materials cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Calculate gravel, pipe, filter fabric and cost for a French drain of any length.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A French drain moves groundwater away from a foundation or soggy yard using a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe. Getting the quantities right matters, because the pipe, filter fabric and clean gravel are all bought separately.

This calculator subtracts the volume of the pipe from the trench, so you do not over-order gravel, and calculates the fabric needed to wrap the whole trench with an overlap.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length of the drain, and the trench width and depth.
Choose the pipe diameter, usually 4 inches.
Add a small allowance for extra pipe and gravel.
Enter local prices to see a materials cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Trench volume = length × width × depth
Gravel volume = trench volume − pipe volume
Fabric = length × (2 × depth + width + 12 in overlap)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A 50 ft drain that is 12 inches wide and 24 inches deep has a trench volume of 100 cubic feet. After subtracting about 4.4 cubic feet for the pipe and adding 10%, you need about 3.9 cubic yards, or 5.5 tons, of gravel, 55 ft of pipe and roughly 330 sq ft of fabric. Materials cost about $482 at the default prices.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Slope the trench about 1% (one inch of fall every eight feet) toward a safe outlet.
Use clean washed stone, and place the pipe with the holes facing down.
Wrap the stone, not the pipe, with filter fabric to keep silt out.
Check where the water will exit. Do not drain onto a neighbor's land.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much gravel do I need for a French drain?
default.a: Multiply trench length, width and depth to get cubic feet, subtract the pipe volume, and convert to cubic yards and tons. The calculator does this and adds an allowance.

default.q: How deep should a French drain be?
default.a: Often 18 to 36 inches. It should be deep enough to intercept the water, with a continuous downward slope to the outlet.

default.q: What size pipe should I use?
default.a: Four-inch perforated pipe is the common choice for residential drains. Larger pipe can be used for long runs or heavy flows.

default.q: Does a French drain need filter fabric?
default.a: In most soils, yes. Fabric keeps fine soil from clogging the stone and pipe over time.

seo.title: Retaining Wall Block Calculator: Blocks, Caps & Gravel
seo.description: Free retaining wall block calculator. Enter wall length, height and block size to estimate wall blocks, cap blocks, backfill gravel and materials cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate wall blocks, cap blocks, drainage gravel and materials cost for a segmental retaining wall.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A segmental retaining wall is built from stacked blocks on a compacted gravel base, with drainage gravel behind it. Block count depends on both the wall's size and the face dimensions of your chosen block.

This calculator counts courses and blocks per course, includes buried base courses, adds cap blocks, and estimates the base and backfill gravel and materials cost.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the wall length and visible height.
Enter the face width and height of your block, and the length of the cap block.
Set the number of buried base courses and an allowance for cuts.
Enter the gravel backfill and base dimensions, and the unit prices.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Courses = ceil(height × 12 ÷ block height) + buried courses
Blocks per course = ceil(length × 12 ÷ block width)
Gravel = (length × height × backfill width) + (length × base width × base depth)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A 30 ft long wall that is 3 ft high with 16 × 6 inch blocks has 6 visible courses plus 1 buried course, and 23 blocks per course. With 8% for cuts that is 174 blocks, plus 30 cap blocks. The base and backfill take about 4.4 cubic yards (6.2 tons) of gravel. Materials come to roughly $1,183 at the default prices.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Many codes require a permit and an engineer above about 4 feet, measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall. Some places set the limit lower, and walls that carry a slope, driveway or building above often need engineering at any height.
Always add drainage gravel and a drain pipe behind the wall. Water pressure is the main cause of failures.
Buy a few extra blocks, and from the same production lot, to avoid color differences.

fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How many blocks do I need for a retaining wall?
default.a: Divide the wall's face area by one block's face area, or count courses and blocks per course. Add buried base courses and about 5% to 10% for cuts and breakage.

default.q: How much gravel do I need behind a retaining wall?
default.a: Typically a 12 inch wide column of clean gravel behind the full wall height, plus a compacted gravel base under the first course.

default.q: How tall can a DIY retaining wall be?
default.a: Model building codes commonly require a permit and engineered design above about 4 feet, measured from the footing to the top of the wall, and many towns set a lower limit of 2 to 3 feet. Walls that support a slope, driveway or building, and tiered walls, may need engineering even when they are shorter. Ask your local building department.

default.a: Caps finish the top, hide hollow cores and are glued in place. Count one per cap length along the wall.

seo.title: Excavation Volume Calculator: Cubic Yards & Truck Loads
seo.description: Free excavation volume calculator. Enter length, width and depth to get cubic yards in place, loose volume after swell, weight in tons and number of truck loads.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Convert an excavation's length, width and depth to bank yards, loose yards, tons and truck loads.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Digging a hole removes a measurable volume of soil, but that soil takes up more space once it is loosened. Excavators work from in-place (bank) yards, while trucks carry loose yards, so both numbers matter.

This calculator converts the size of the excavation into bank volume, applies a swell factor to find the loose volume, and estimates the weight and number of truck loads.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length, width and depth of the excavation in feet.
Choose a swell factor for your soil type.
Enter the loose weight of the soil and the capacity of your trucks.
Read the bank volume, loose volume, loads and weight.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Bank cubic yards = length × width × depth ÷ 27
Loose cubic yards = bank yards × (1 + swell)
Truck loads = loose yards ÷ truck capacity (rounded up)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A 40 × 30 ft excavation 4 feet deep contains 177.8 cubic yards in place. With a 25% swell it becomes 222.2 loose cubic yards, weighing about 289 tons at 1.3 tons per yard, which is 23 loads in a 10 yd³ truck.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Swell is higher in clay and lower in sand and gravel. Use your geotechnical report if you have one.
Excavations with sloped sides contain more soil than vertical ones. Add them to your dimensions.
Call 811 before you dig to locate buried utilities.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate cubic yards of dirt?
default.a: Multiply length, width and depth in feet to get cubic feet, then divide by 27.

default.q: What is the swell factor in excavation?
default.a: It is the percentage by which soil expands when dug. Common soil swells about 25%, clay about 25% to 40% depending on moisture, and sand or gravel roughly 10% to 15%.

default.q: How many cubic yards does a dump truck hold?

seo.title: Compound Interest Calculator: Growth With Monthly Contributions
seo.description: Free compound interest calculator. Enter a starting balance, monthly contribution, rate and years to see your future balance, interest earned and value in today's money.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: See how a starting balance and regular contributions grow over time with compound interest.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Left alone, a balance grows faster each year, which is why starting early and contributing regularly matters more than the exact starting amount.

This calculator models a starting balance plus monthly contributions at your chosen rate and compounding frequency. It shows the future balance, how much of it is your own money and how much is interest, and adjusts for inflation to show the result in today's money.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your starting balance and the amount you will add each month.
Enter the expected annual interest rate and how often interest compounds.
Set the number of years and an inflation estimate.
Read the future balance, the chart and the year-by-year table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Each month: balance = balance × (1 + monthly rate) + contribution
Monthly rate = (1 + annual rate ÷ periods per year)^(periods ÷ 12) − 1
Value in today's money = future balance ÷ (1 + inflation)^years
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: Starting with $10,000 and adding $500 a month at 6% compounded monthly for 20 years grows to about $264,122. You contribute $130,000 and earn $134,122 in interest. After 2.5% yearly inflation, that is worth about $161,186 in today's money.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Time matters most. Adding years has a larger effect than adding a similar amount late.
Rates of return are not guaranteed. Test a lower rate to see a cautious case.
Fees reduce your effective return. Subtract them from the rate you enter.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How is compound interest calculated?
default.a: Interest is added to the balance at each compounding period, and the next period's interest is calculated on the larger balance. With regular contributions, each deposit also starts earning interest.

default.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
default.a: Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount. Compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus all interest earned so far, so it grows faster over time.

default.q: What is the rule of 72?
default.a: Dividing 72 by the annual rate gives a rough number of years to double your money. At 6%, it takes about 12 years.

default.q: Does compounding more often make a big difference?
default.a: Slightly. Monthly versus yearly compounding at the same rate adds a small amount. The rate and the time period matter much more.

This calculator gives you the target amount for each category and compares them with what you actually spend, so you can see where to adjust.

Wants target = take-home income × 30%
Savings and debt target = take-home income × 20%

fields.label: Tagline

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
An emergency fund is money set aside for job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs, so you do not have to borrow at high interest. How much you need depends on your essential expenses and how stable your income is.

This calculator sets a target based on months of expenses, shows how many months you already have covered, and estimates how long it will take to close the gap with regular savings and interest.

Read the target, the shortfall and the time to reach it.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.default:

Each month: balance = balance × (1 + monthly rate) + contribution
Months covered = current savings ÷ essential monthly expenses

fields.label: Worked example

Count only essentials, not every expense. You can cut the rest in an emergency.
Keep the fund in an easily accessible insured account, not in volatile investments.

default.q: How much emergency fund do I need?

default.q: Should I build an emergency fund or pay off debt first?
default.a: Many people build a small starter fund first, then pay down high-interest debt, then grow the fund. The right order depends on your situation.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate your monthly car payment, total interest and the full cost of financing a vehicle.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A car payment depends on more than the sticker price. Sales tax, dealer fees, your down payment and trade-in, the interest rate and the length of the loan all change what you pay each month and in total.

This calculator builds the amount financed from the price, tax and fees, subtracts your down payment and trade-in, and shows your monthly payment, total interest and the full cost of the vehicle. A table compares terms from 36 to 84 months.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the vehicle price, your down payment and any trade-in value.
Enter the loan rate (APR) and the term in months.
Enter sales tax and any title, registration or dealer fees.

fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Amount financed = price − trade-in + sales tax + fees − down payment
Monthly payment = loan × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months
Total interest = monthly payment × months − amount financed
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A $32,000 car with $4,000 down, a $3,000 trade-in, 6.5% sales tax on the price after trade-in and $600 of fees means financing $27,485. At 7% over 60 months the payment is about $544 a month, with $5,169 of interest. The whole vehicle costs about $39,654 including your down payment and trade-in. Stretching to 84 months lowers the payment to about $415 but raises interest to roughly $7,360.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
A longer term lowers the payment but increases interest and the time you owe more than the car is worth.
Get a pre-approved rate from a bank or credit union before visiting a dealer.
Look at the total cost, not just the monthly payment.
Results are estimates from the numbers you enter. Dealer quotes, lender terms, taxes and fees vary, so confirm with the dealer or lender before you sign.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How is a car payment calculated?
default.a: The lender takes the amount financed, the interest rate and the term, and uses the standard loan formula to find the level monthly payment that pays off the loan.

default.q: How much car can I afford?
default.a: A common guideline is to put 20% down, finance for no more than four years and keep total car costs under 10% of gross income. These are rules of thumb, not requirements.

default.q: Does a bigger down payment help?
default.a: Yes. It reduces the amount financed, so you pay less interest and have a lower payment. It also reduces the risk of owing more than the car is worth.

default.a: Often yes, if you roll it into the financing. This calculator includes tax and fees in the amount financed.

seo.description: Free auto lease calculator. Enter price, MSRP, residual value, money factor, term and tax to estimate your monthly lease payment, equivalent APR and total lease cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate a monthly lease payment from the price, residual value, money factor and term.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A lease payment covers the part of the car's value you use up, plus a finance charge and tax. The terms dealers quote, money factor and residual value, are not as familiar as an interest rate, which makes leases hard to compare.

This calculator turns those terms into a monthly payment. It shows the depreciation and finance charge separately, converts the money factor into an approximate APR and totals the cost of the lease.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the MSRP and the negotiated price of the car.
Enter your down payment and any acquisition fees.
Enter the residual value as a percentage of MSRP, the money factor and the lease term.
Enter the sales tax rate on lease payments.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Capitalized cost = negotiated price + fees − down payment
Depreciation per month = (capitalized cost − residual value) ÷ months
Finance charge per month = (capitalized cost + residual value) × money factor
Payment = (depreciation + finance charge) × (1 + tax rate)
Approximate APR = money factor × 2,400
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A car with a $36,000 MSRP negotiated to $35,000, with $2,000 down, $695 in fees, a 60% residual ($21,600), a 0.0025 money factor (about 6% APR) and a 36-month term has a capitalized cost of $33,695. Depreciation is about $336 a month and the finance charge about $138. With 6.5% tax the payment is about $505 a month, and the lease costs about $20,181 including the down payment.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Negotiate the price of the car, not just the monthly payment. A lower capitalized cost lowers the payment.
Ask for the money factor and residual value in writing and convert the factor to APR.
Check the mileage allowance and the fees for excess miles and wear.
Results are estimates from the numbers you enter. Dealer quotes, lender terms, taxes and fees vary, so confirm with the dealer or lender before you sign.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is a money factor?
default.a: It is the lease's finance rate expressed as a small decimal. Multiply it by 2,400 to get an approximate APR, so 0.0025 is about 6%.

default.q: What is a residual value?
default.a: It is what the leasing company expects the car to be worth at the end of the lease, usually expressed as a percentage of MSRP. A higher residual means lower depreciation and a lower payment.

default.q: Is leasing cheaper than buying?
default.a: Leasing usually has lower monthly payments, but you do not own the car at the end. Buying often costs less over many years if you keep the car long term.

default.q: Do I pay tax on a lease?
default.a: Rules differ by state. Some tax each monthly payment, some tax the whole price upfront. Enter the rate that applies to your payment.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate how much value a car loses each year and what it may be worth when you sell.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Depreciation is usually the largest cost of owning a new car, and it happens quietly. A car loses the most value in its first year and keeps losing value each year after, though more slowly.

This calculator applies a first-year rate and a yearly rate for later years to estimate the car's value over the time you own it, and expresses the loss as a monthly cost.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.default:
Enter the purchase price.

Value after later years = previous value × (1 − yearly rate)

fields.label: Worked example

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Convert between cost, price, markup and gross margin, and find the price for a target margin.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Markup and margin both describe profit, but they use different bases, and mixing them up is a common and costly pricing mistake. Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price.

This calculator shows both for the cost and price you enter, shows total gross profit at your sales volume, and lists the selling price you need to hit target margins.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the cost to you of each unit.
Enter the price you sell it for.
Enter the number of units you expect to sell.
Use the table to see the price needed for different margins.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Profit = selling price − cost
Margin = profit ÷ selling price
Markup = profit ÷ cost
Price for a target margin = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: An item costing $60 and selling for $100 earns $40 profit. That is a 40% margin (40 ÷ 100) but a 66.7% markup (40 ÷ 60). Selling 200 units earns $8,000 gross profit. To reach a 50% margin on a $60 cost, the price must be $120.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
A 50% markup is not a 50% margin. A 50% markup gives a 33.3% margin.
Gross margin ignores overhead. Check that it covers rent, salaries and other costs.
Review prices regularly as costs change.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is the difference between markup and margin?

default.q: How do I calculate a selling price from a margin?
default.a: Divide your cost by one minus the margin. For a $60 cost and a 40% margin, the price is $60 ÷ 0.60 = $100.

default.q: What is a good profit margin?
default.a: It varies by industry. Retail often works with gross margins of 20% to 50%, while software can be far higher. Compare with your sector and your overheads.

seo.title: Break-Even Calculator: Break-Even Units & Revenue
seo.description: Free break-even calculator. Enter fixed costs, price and variable cost per unit to find break-even units and sales, and the volume needed for a target profit.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Find how many units you must sell to cover costs, and how many to reach a profit target.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
The break-even point is the sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs. Below it you lose money, above it you make a profit. It is one of the first numbers to know before launching or pricing a product.

This calculator divides your fixed costs by the contribution each unit makes after variable costs. It shows the units and sales needed to break even, the volume for a profit target, and a chart of profit at different volumes.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your fixed costs for the period, for example per month.
Enter the selling price and the variable cost of each unit.
Enter the profit you want to earn.
Read the break-even volume and the chart.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
Break-even sales = break-even units × selling price
Units for a profit target = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: With $12,000 of monthly fixed costs, a $45 price and $18 of variable cost, each unit contributes $27. You break even at about 445 units, or about $20,000 of sales. To earn $3,000 a month you need to sell about 556 units.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Include every fixed cost, such as rent, wages, insurance, software and loan payments.
Raising price or cutting variable cost lowers the break-even point quickly.
Check that the break-even volume is realistic for your market.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate the break-even point?

default.q: What are fixed and variable costs?

seo.title: Sales Tax Calculator: Add or Remove Tax From a Price
seo.description: Free sales tax calculator. Enter a price and tax rate to see the sales tax and total, or find the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive amount, with a table of rates.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Add sales tax to a price, or work out the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive total.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Sales tax is added at the register in most US states, but rates differ by state, county and city, and some items are exempt. Knowing how to add it, and how to take it back out of a total, is useful for shoppers and small businesses.

This calculator adds tax to a pre-tax price and quantity, shows the total, works out the pre-tax price if the number you entered already includes tax, and compares totals at different rates.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the price before tax and the quantity.
Enter the combined sales tax rate for your location.
Read the tax and total, and the pre-tax price if the entered price already includes tax.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Sales tax = price × quantity × tax rate
Total = price × quantity + sales tax
Pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive price = price ÷ (1 + tax rate)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A $249.99 item at an 8.25% sales tax rate has about $20.62 of tax, for a total of $270.61. If $249.99 already included the tax, the pre-tax price would be about $230.94.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use the combined state and local rate for your exact location.
Check whether your goods or services are taxable. Rules vary by product and jurisdiction.
Businesses that sell across states may have registration obligations. Ask an accountant.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate sales tax?
default.a: Multiply the price by the tax rate as a decimal. For 8.25%, multiply by 0.0825. Add that to the price for the total.

default.q: How do I remove sales tax from a total?
default.a: Divide the total by one plus the tax rate. For a total of $270.61 at 8.25%, divide by 1.0825 to get $249.99.

default.q: Is sales tax the same everywhere?
default.a: No. Rates differ by state, county and city, and some places have no state sales tax. Check your local rate.

seo.title: Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator: What Should You Charge?
seo.description: Free freelance hourly rate calculator. Enter your income goal, expenses, tax set-aside, billable hours and time off to find the hourly rate you need to charge.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out the hourly rate you need to charge to reach your income goal after expenses and tax.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Freelancers often set rates by looking at an employee's hourly pay, but that leaves out business expenses, taxes, unpaid time off and the hours spent finding clients and doing admin. As a result, many freelancers undercharge.

This calculator works backward from the income you want to take home. It adds taxes and expenses to find the revenue you need, then divides by your real billable hours to give an hourly rate.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the yearly take-home income you want.
Enter your yearly business expenses and the share of profit you set aside for tax and retirement.
Enter the billable hours you work per week and the weeks you take off.
Read the hourly rate and the revenue target, and compare different billable hours.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Profit needed = take-home income ÷ (1 − tax set-aside)
Revenue needed = profit needed + business expenses
Hourly rate = revenue needed ÷ (billable hours per week × weeks worked)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: To take home $70,000 with 25% set aside for tax, you need about $93,333 of profit. Add $8,000 of expenses and you need about $101,333 of revenue. Billing 25 hours a week for 46 weeks is 1,150 hours, so you would charge about $88.12 an hour.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Count only billable hours. Sales, admin and learning rarely fit inside client time.
Include unpaid holidays, sick days and slow periods in your weeks off.
Consider project or value-based pricing once you know your minimum hourly rate.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much should a freelancer charge per hour?
default.a: Enough to cover your income goal, business expenses, taxes and unpaid time. This calculator shows the rate that does that for your numbers.

default.q: Why is a freelance rate higher than an employee's hourly rate?
default.a: Freelancers pay their own taxes, insurance and expenses, have no paid time off and cannot bill every working hour.

default.q: How many hours can a freelancer bill in a week?
default.a: Many freelancers bill 20 to 30 hours in a full working week. The rest goes to admin, marketing and finding work.

seo.title: Business Loan Calculator: Payment, Interest & Total Cost
seo.description: Free business loan calculator. Enter the loan amount, rate, term and origination fee to see your monthly payment, total interest, cash received and cost by term.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate monthly payments, total interest and fees on a term loan for your business.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A business loan can fund equipment, stock or expansion, but the monthly payment, interest and fees all reduce the benefit. Knowing the full cost helps you decide how much to borrow and for how long.

This calculator works out the monthly payment on a fixed-rate term loan, the total interest, the origination fee deducted from your proceeds, and the cash you actually receive. A table compares different terms.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the loan amount, interest rate and term in years.
Enter the origination fee as a percentage.
Review the monthly payment, total interest and cash received.
Compare terms in the table to find a payment you can afford.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Monthly payment = loan × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months
Total interest = monthly payment × months − loan amount
Cash received = loan amount − origination fee
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default: A $50,000 loan at 9% over 5 years has a monthly payment of about $1,038 and costs about $12,275 in interest. With a 2% origination fee of $1,000 you receive $49,000, so the total cost of the loan is about $13,275.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Compare the total cost, not only the rate. Fees can add significantly.
Check for prepayment penalties and whether payments are monthly, weekly or daily.
Make sure the loan's payments fit your cash flow, with room for a slow month.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate a business loan payment?
default.a: Use the standard loan formula with the amount, interest rate and number of monthly payments. The calculator does this for you.

default.q: What is an origination fee?
default.a: A fee the lender charges for processing the loan, usually a percentage of the amount and often deducted from the money you receive.

default.q: Does a longer term save money?
default.a: A longer term lowers the monthly payment but increases total interest. Use the table to compare.
